## TL;DR

I found a test-side scheduling window in the reported holder/waiter test. Its five-second polling deadline could expire before the spawned shell was scheduled to write the marker, even though the test itself allows 30 seconds. I replaced that poll with a marker emitted by the holder after it has acquired the lock and written its start record. The waiter is now launched only after that event. No production lock behavior changed.

Both reported lock tests passed 20 consecutive repetitions under two local CPU load processes. The full 166-test file passed 20 consecutive times idle and 20 consecutive times under the same load. The scoped RepoOS check also passed remotely on thinkpad. The original host, bee, was not selected by the configured remote validation pool in this run.

## Work and rationale

I read `docs/debugging-check-failures.md` and inspected the host lock shell plus both reported tests. Each test creates its lock root under a unique `mkdtemp` directory, so parallel tests do not share their lock slots or queue entries. The lock shell’s timeout and stale-entry behavior is exercised through actual child shell processes; there was no evidence that production lock state or filesystem sharing caused this failure.

The holder/waiter case used `sh(holder)` and then polled a marker file every 20 ms for at most five seconds. That marker is created only after the spawned shell starts, acquires the lock, and begins its inner command. The five-second cap was unrelated to the 30-second test timeout and therefore measured child scheduling latency as well as lock correctness. The intended assertion is only meaningful once the holder owns the slot. I changed the holder’s inner command to emit a unique stdout marker after recording `start`, and the test now waits for that event before invoking the waiter. If the holder exits before producing the marker, the test reports its captured output. The release file is written in `finally`, and the holder process is awaited there so a failed assertion does not leave it behind.

The lock roots remain isolated per test and the two contender processes still share the same lock root within the test. That preserves the cross-process behavior being tested. The existing #1101 stale dead-PID test was not changed. No change was made to shell deadlines, host lock production code, or the validation gate.

## Approaches tried

- Read the repository’s check-failure guidance and the focused test and production shell implementation.
- Ran the original holder/waiter case 20 times in isolation before the edit. It passed each time, consistent with the reported intermittent nature.
- Replaced the fixed polling window with a holder-generated event, preserving the test’s lock ownership and timeout assertions.
- Ran the holder/waiter test and the #1101 stale dead-PID queue test together 20 consecutive times while two `yes` processes consumed CPU. Both tests passed in every repetition.
- Ran the complete `remote-host-pool.test.ts` file 20 consecutive times idle (3,320 test executions) and 20 consecutive times under two local CPU load processes (another 3,320 test executions). Every run passed.
- Ran `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. The remote runner selected thinkpad, built the candidate, and passed all six selected test files (262 tests), including all 166 tests in this file and both reported cases. The browser gate passed. Local format, lint, build, CSS, contrast, UI smoke, and other applicable guards also passed.

## Challenges and blockers

The reported red gate happened on bee, but this run’s configured remote pool selected thinkpad. I could not compare bee’s shell, filesystem, clock, or load characteristics directly. The check did exercise the remote validation path on a different host and passed. The root cause here is inferred from the test’s own five-second startup deadline and the intended ordering; the original bee failure was not reproduced. Full-file repetition took about a minute per pass locally, so the 40 additional passes took roughly 40 minutes. The remote gate itself ran the complete file once.

## Key learnings

Test synchronization should depend on the state under test, not a short polling allowance for when a child process happens to get CPU. A marker emitted after lock acquisition makes the ordering explicit and keeps the contention test meaningful under runner load. The per-test temporary lock roots rule out shared test-worker lock state for these cases. The evidence points to test setup timing, not a production lock defect; remote success on thinkpad is useful coverage but does not establish bee-specific filesystem or load behavior.
